name: Mingang Doso
confidence_why: One first-hand description, checked against the source; 3 other works consulted do not discuss stress.
catalog_citation: Benson, Peace & Alexander Andrason. 2022. A Living Grammar Sketch of Mingang Doso, Version 1.1. Salem, OR: Living Tongues Institute for Endangered Languages. 30 pp. CC BY 4.0.
catalog_quote: Like most Adamawa languages, Mingang Doso is a tonal language and exhibits complex tonal structures. The following tones can be distinguished: high tone [ ́], mid tone [ ̄], and low tone [ ̀], as well as mid falling [ ̂] and, especially in rhetorical questions, low rising [ ᷅]. The tonal patterns are associated with each lexeme and thus the tone is a lexical property of a word. Specific tonal patterns are also exploited to mark questions or communicate certain emotive nuances, e.g., surprise.
world_status: statement found in an open source

new_statements.second_reader_evidence: Opened (30 pp., text, the PDF's metadata OK). The quoted passage is on printed p. 7 = p. 9, under heading "2.3 Tone", exactly as quoted (three short paragraphs in the PDF, joined in the quote; wording, tone diacritics and "e.g., surprise." all match). Surrounding section read: §2 "Phonetics" = 2.1 Consonants (pp. 5-6, notes syllabic [n̩], consonants word-initial/medial only, finals limited to m, ŋ, j, w), 2.2 Vowels (p. 6, oral + nasal inventories), 2.3 Tone (p. 7); §3 Morpho-syntax starts p. 8. extracted text of the whole sketch a full-text search for stress/accent|accent|prosod|syllab|intonat|supraseg|vowel length: only hits are "syllabic [n̩]" and "monosyllabic/disyllabic verbs" (p. ~22)…
new_statements.rule_in_words: The only phonological description states that Mingang Doso is a tonal language with lexically specified tone (H, M, L, mid-falling, low-rising); it makes no statement at all about word stress or accent, so no stress position can be assigned from the literature.
new_statements.exceptions: None on stress; on tone, question/emotive intonation overlays are noted. Norton & Othaniel 2020 (p. 43) add that H and L tones are switched in Doso relative to other Jen varieties (except H after voiced obstruents).
new_statements.domain_note: Tone is stated to be a property of the lexeme (word level); question/emotive tonal patterns operate at the utterance level. The sketch's 'Phonetics' section (consonants, vowels, tone) is under 3 pages, and stress is simply absent from it; it does not explicitly deny word stress.
new_statements.identity_note: Benson & Andrason 2022 describe the speech of Munga village (Bunkaubu, Bugbamui, Mundang quarters), Karim-Lamido LGA, Taraba State — i.e. Mingang Doso proper (ming1254 / mko). Norton & Othaniel 2020 label the same variety 'Doso'; Kleinewillinghöfer 2015 labels it 'MIN = Munga [Məngaŋ] Doso'. Not to be confused with Munga Leelau (LE in Kleinewillinghöfer), a different Bikwin language also called Munga.

tone_statements.quote: Second, each onomatopoeia has its own lexical tonal pattern. Of course, this property is not extra-systematic as both Dza and Mingang Doso are tonal languages with complex tonal configurations – as is the case of all Jen cluster varieties more generally. Interestingly, no tonal tendencies can be discerned in the onomatopoeic material collected and no tonal patterns seem to be limited to onomatopoeias either.
tone_statements.summary: Lexical tone (each lexeme, incl. onomatopoeias, has its own tonal pattern); 'complex tonal configurations'; inventory not restated (H/M/L + mid-falling + low-rising per the 2022 sketch); nothing on stress.

sources.note: Section 2 'Phonetics' has 2.1 Consonants, 2.2 Vowels, 2.3 Tone (p. 7). States the language is tonal (H, M, L, mid-falling, low-rising) and that tone is a lexical property of each word; questions/emotive nuances use tonal patterns. The words stress/accent/prosody do not occur anywhere in the sketch; no statement on word stress.

sources.citation: Norton, Russell & Nlabephee K. Othaniel. 2020. The Jen language cluster: a comparative analysis of wordlists. Language in Africa 1(3): 17-99. doi:10.37892/2686-8946-2020-1-3-17-99
sources.note: Comparative phonology of ten Jen varieties incl. Doso (= Mingang Doso, Othaniel's 300-item wordlist). Section 3.3 Tone (pp. 43-45): 'High, mid, low, falling and rising tones were noted.. High and low tones are switched in Doso, except that H does not become L after a voiced obstruent.' Abstract lists nasalisation, tone and breathiness as the prosodic features. No mention of stress or accent anywhere (a full-text search for stress/accent found nothing).

sources.quote: Second, each onomatopoeia has its own lexical tonal pattern. Of course, this property is not extra-systematic as both Dza and Mingang Doso are tonal languages with complex tonal configurations – as is the case of all Jen cluster varieties more generally. sources.note: §3.1.2 Phonetics states that Mingang Doso (like Dza and all Jen varieties) is a tonal language with complex tonal configurations and that every onomatopoeia carries its own lexical tonal pattern; onomatopoeias additionally use extra-long vowels and special intonation/melody. No tone inventory is given here (the same authors' 2022 sketch, the works listed here, gives H, M, L, mid-falling, low-rising); all 136 forms in the tables are tone-marked.
